items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 6.6 Shells of sea creatures such as limpets are made of calcium carbonate, CaCO3. If they were 100% pure, 1 g of shells would react with hydrochloric acid to give 0.24 dm³ of carbon dioxide.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: Another way of thinking about this is that to go from 3 (H₂) to 2 (Al) we divide the 3 by 3 to get 1 and then multiply this by 2 to get 2. In other words, to go from the number of moles of H2 to the number of moles of Al, we divide the number of moles of H2 by 3 and then multiply by 2.

items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: The equation to calculate the mass is the number of moles × mass of 1 mol. It is important to multiply by 27 here and not 54. Although it is 2Al in the equation, we have already used the 2 in calculating the number of moles of Al. Also, the mass of 0.00278 mol of Al must always be the same, it cannot depend on what it is reacting with. 0.00278mol of Al always contains the same number of atoms.

items.label: section_header
items.text: CONCENTRATIONS OF SOLUTIONS

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: You may also find the symbol M used. For example, dilute hydrochloric acid might have a concentration quoted as 2 M. M means 'mol/dm³' and is described as the molarity of the solution. You can also read 2M as '2 molar'.

items.label: text
items.text: From the chemical equation we can see that 1 mol of CaCO₃ produces 1 mol of CO2 so we know that 0.0100 mol of CaCO₃ will produce the same number of moles of CO2, that is, 0.0100 mol.

items.label: text
items.text: We now need to work out the volume occupied by 0.0100 mol of CO2:

items.label: formula
items.text: v o l u m e o f g a s & = \text {number of moles } \times \text {molar volume} \\ & = 0 . 0 1 0 0 \times 2 4 = 0 . 2 4 d m ^ { 3 }

items.label: text
items.text: We have used the molar volume in dm³ and so our answer will be in dm³. It is really important to include the units here because the examiner will not know whether you mean cm³or dm³ unless you write it down.

items.label: section_header
items.text: A PROBLEM INVOLVING MAKING HYDROGEN

items.label: text
items.text: Aluminium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid according to the equation

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 A ( s ) + 6 H C l ( a q ) \rightarrow 2 A C l _ { 3 } ( a q ) + 3 H _ { 2 } ( g )

items.label: text
items.text: What mass of aluminium would you need to add to an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid so that you produced 100 cm³ of hydrogen at room temperature and pressure? (A, of Al = 27; molar volume = 24 000 cm³ at rtp.)

items.label: text
items.text: We can only calculate the number of moles of the hydrogen gas. We do not know the mass of aluminium, that is what we are trying to find.

items.label: text
items.text: The volume of hydrogen gas is given in cm³ so we use the molar volume of a gas as 24000 cm3:

items.label: text
items.text: We could also write this number in standard form as 4.17 × 10-3 mol.

items.label: text
items.text: Looking at the chemical equation we can see that 3 mol of H2is produced from 2 mol of Al (we are only looking at the big numbers in front of the formulae). So we can see that the number of moles of Al will be 213 times the number of moles of H2.

items.label: text
items.text: The number of moles of aluminium required to produce 0.00417 mol of H2 is 0.00417× 213 = 0.00278mol.

items.label: text
items.text: We can convert this to a mass by using the equation:

items.label: text
items.text: mass = number of moles × mass of 1 mol

items.label: text
items.text: These can also be written as g dm-3 and moldm-3. You read them as grams per cubic decimetre' and 'moles per cubic decimetre'. Remember: 1 cubic decimetre is the same as 1 litre.
